name: Variable Binding
why: Assigning a value to a name lets you store data in memory and refer to it repeatedly without recalculating or retyping it.

name: Data Structures
why: Grouping related values into collections like vectors, lists, or tables allows you to organize and work with multiple data points together.

name: Indexing
why: Using a position, name, or condition allows you to look up, extract, or update specific elements inside a collection.

name: Boolean Logic
why: Evaluating expressions into true or false outcomes allows programs to make decisions and control which code runs.

name: Equality Comparison
why: Checking whether two values are identical lets your code verify expectations and branch based on whether data matches.

name: Type Coercion
why: When an operation expects one kind of data but receives another, the language may quietly convert it behind the scenes, sometimes causing subtle surprises.

name: Scope
why: Scope sets the boundaries where a variable exists and can be seen, preventing names used in one part of a program from accidentally overwriting names elsewhere.

name: Function Definition
why: Packaging a set of instructions into a reusable named block lets you run that logic with different inputs without duplicating code.

name: Closure
why: A function carries the environment it was born in. That means it can use variables that were in scope when it was created, even after that scope has ended.

name: Environment Mutation
why: Modifying variables outside the current local function scope alters shared state, which can create side effects that are hard to trace and debug.

name: Module System
why: Packaging code into separate libraries or modules lets you reuse external functionality while keeping distinct namespaces so names do not collide.

name: Search Path
why: When you write a bare name, the runtime looks through an ordered sequence of environments and loaded packages to decide which matching definition wins.

name: Iteration
why: Repeating a set of actions across a collection or until a target is reached automates repetitive work instead of writing the same steps over and over.

name: Vectorisation
why: Applying an operation to an entire collection at once lets the computer process all items together without writing a manual loop.

name: Recycling
why: When an operation pairs collections of different lengths, the runtime repeats elements from the shorter one to match the longer one.

name: Pipe Chaining
why: Directing the output of one step straight into the input of the next lets you read data transformations in a clear, left-to-right flow.

name: Mutability
why: Determines whether changing a collection alters the original data everywhere it is referenced, or creates an independent copy with the changes.

name: Missing Data
why: Representing absent or unknown observations with dedicated placeholders prevents missing values from being confused with real data like zero or false.

name: Error Handling
why: Catching unexpected issues as they occur allows your program to recover gracefully or give a helpful explanation rather than crashing abruptly.

name: String Manipulation
why: Examining, splicing, formatting, and searching pieces of text lets programs clean messy input and generate readable messages.
